title: The glory comes to Babylon
sum: Ezekiel is a priest among the exiles, far from the Temple he would have served. By the Kebar canal the sky opens, and a storm cloud comes from the north with fire and a gleam like glowing metal. Four living creatures with four faces and four wings carry a platform; beside each is a wheel full of eyes; above them is a dome like ice, a blue throne, and a figure like a human on it, wrapped in fire and a rainbow.

Every description is hedged: it is the likeness, the look, the appearance. What Ezekiel says he saw was 'the likeness of the glory of the LORD', and he falls on his face. The chapter says that the LORD is not tied to the Temple. His throne moves, and it has come to the exiles.
readings: Read as a vision of the throne-chariot

The text is a prophet's call vision, like Isaiah 6, given the form of the royal throne carried by cherubim in the Temple's Holy of Holies. The LORD travels, and so the exile is not out of his reach. This is the reading that stays closest to how the book itself uses the vision (10:1-22; 43:1-5).
Read as a picture drawn from Babylon

Mesopotamian palaces and temples had guardian creatures that mixed human, lion, bull and eagle features, and storm gods in cloud and fire. Ezekiel, living among these, may have drawn on that world to say that the LORD outshines their gods. Othmar Keel has compared the vision with seals and carvings of the ancient Near East.
Read as a secret to be guarded

Jewish tradition made the 'Account of the Chariot' a hidden teaching that the Mishnah limits to one wise student at a time, and later mystics tried to ascend to the throne themselves. The chapter is therefore both a public reading on Shavuot and a restricted study.

views.H: Dated to 593 BC, five years after the exile began and five years before the final siege. The vision comes when the exiles still hope for a short stay and a safe Jerusalem.
views.C: Some scholars think the wheels (1:15-21) were added later, because they interrupt the movement from the living creatures to the dome. Zimmerli finds additions in the chapter; Greenberg reads the whole as one design.
views.J: The haftarah for the first day of Shavuot (1:1-28; 3:12). The Targum expands the chapter; the sages wondered whether to read it in public at all. The 'Chariot' is a study for the few (Mishnah Hagigah 2:1), and the Talmud has the story of the boy and the fire (Hagigah 13a).
views.X: The four faces are the four Gospels in Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.11.8) and in Jerome, with different matchings; the throne vision stands behind Revelation 4. Gregory the Great's first homilies on Ezekiel begin here.
views.F: Little in this chapter is read as future; some dispensational and other writers look for the return of this glory in Ezekiel 43 and in the age to come.

deep.h: What was read for this part
deep.b: The Plain is made from the Leningrad Codex of the Hebrew. For chapters 1 to 7 the Dead Sea Scrolls that preserve verses are 11QEzek (1:8-10; 4:3-6, 9-10; 5:11-17; 7:9-12), 4QEzek-b (1:10-13, 16-24; no text of 1:15 survives and only a few words of 1:20) and 1QEzek (4:16-5:1), read through the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcriptions. No scroll preserves the other verses of these chapters. The Greek was read in Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus; the critical editions of Rahlfs and Ziegler and the studies of Lust and Tov are cited only as reported by others. Rashi was read on Sefaria for a few verses.

Ezekiel counts years from the exile of Jehoiachin in 597 BC, the same system as 2 Kings. The first year of the exile ran from spring 597 to spring 596, so the fifth year (1:2) is 593 BC. The book gives thirteen dates:

1:1-2, 593 BC (fifth year, fourth month, fifth day); 8:1, 592 (sixth year, sixth month, fifth day); 20:1, 591 (seventh year); 24:1, 588 (ninth year, tenth month, tenth day: the day the siege began, 2 Kings 25:1); 26:1, 587/586 (eleventh year); 29:1, 588/587 (tenth year, tenth month, twelfth day); 29:17, 571 (twenty-seventh year, the latest in the book); 30:20, 587/586 (eleventh year); 31:1, 587/586 (eleventh year); 32:1 and 32:17, 586/585 (twelfth year); 33:21, 586/585 (twelfth year, tenth month, fifth day); 40:1, 573 (twenty-fifth year).

The fall of Jerusalem is 586 BC on this site; some scholars date it 587, and the dates of the exile years can differ by a year depending on whether the years are counted from spring or autumn (see John Hayes and Paul Hooker, and Edwin Thiele, on the counting of Kings). The book is not in strict date order: 29:17 is out of place beside the oracles from 587/586.

The book opens with 'the thirtieth year' and never says what is being counted. The oldest answer is the prophet's age, held by Origen and Jerome. Rashi says that the holy spirit inserted the next verse, which names the fifth year of the exile, to tell us what the thirtieth year refers to (reported from Sefaria). Other proposals are thirty years from the finding of the law book under Josiah, from a Jubilee, or from the start of the Babylonian era. None of them is certain.

echoes: Isaiah 6:1-8; Daniel 7:9-10; Revelation 4:1-8; Revelation 10:1; Exodus 24:9-11; Psalm 18:7-15; Genesis 9:13-16; Ezekiel 10:1-22; Ezekiel 43:1-5

settings.what: The vision of the glory by the Kebar canal
settings.by: Ezekiel, who tells it in the first person
settings.to: Himself and the exiles at Tel-abib; the report is for the elders who later sit in his house
settings.when: The fifth day of the fourth month of the fifth year of Jehoiachin's exile, 593 BC, five years into the exile and before the siege
settings.why: To tell the exiles that the LORD's throne is not confined to the Temple: it moves, and it has come to Babylon. The vision commissions Ezekiel and prepares for the hard message that the glory will leave Jerusalem (chapters 8-11).
settings.readers: For the exiles who read the book later, the chapter was proof that God was with them in Babylon; for later Jews it became the reading for Shavuot.
views: A priest's call
Greenberg and others treat the vision as the call of a priest, who sees the LORD's throne as the Temple's Holy of Holies, where a priest could never stand.
A prophet's commission (Isaiah 6 and Jeremiah 1)
The chapter plays the role of the call vision in other prophets, with the actual commission in 2:1-3:11.

title: Sent to a rebellious house
sum: The voice from the throne tells the prophet to stand, and a spirit sets him on his feet. He is called 'son of man' for the first time, and sent to the Israelites, 'nations of rebels' who have defied the LORD, they and their ancestors, until today. His hearers are hard in the face and stubborn in heart, and he is to speak whether they listen or not. They will at least know a prophet was among them.
Then a hand holds out a scroll written on both sides with laments, sighing and woe. The prophet is told not to be a rebel himself and to open his mouth and eat.
readings: Read as a call story

The chapter belongs with other call stories: a vision, a commission, an objection met by a promise (Exodus 3-4; Isaiah 6; Jeremiah 1). Ezekiel's differs because he never objects. The commission names the hearers and the cost.
Read as a warning to the prophet
'Do not be rebellious like that rebellious house' (2:8) makes the prophet's own obedience the first test. The hearers may not listen, but the prophet must.

views.H: The 'rebellious house' includes both the exiles and the people in Jerusalem; the historical record of 2 Kings 24 shows a king and a court that had broken faith with Babylon and the LORD.
views.C: Some see 2:1-3:11 as the real call and chapter 1 as an introduction added to it; Zimmerli discusses the layers.
views.J: Rashi gives two reasons for 'son of man': it tells Ezekiel, who has seen the Chariot among the angels, that he is only a human being, and it keeps him from being proud of his closeness to the Chariot (reported from Sefaria).
views.X: The scroll eaten by the prophet is echoed by John in Revelation 10:8-11.

echoes: Jeremiah 1:4-10; Jeremiah 15:16; Isaiah 6:8-13; Revelation 5:1; Revelation 10:8-11; Psalm 8:4; Exodus 32:15

settings.by: The LORD, speaking from the throne
settings.to: Ezekiel, for the sake of the exiles and 'the house of Israel'
settings.when: Immediately after the vision, in 593 BC
settings.why: To send a priest, who expects to serve at the altar, to a people who will not listen. The commission says that his success is not measured by their response, but by their knowing a prophet was there.
settings.readers: For the book's readers after 586, the commission explained why the prophet was ignored and why his words were fulfilled.
views: A single commission
Greenberg reads 1:1-3:15 as one unit: vision, commission, scroll and arrival.
A reworked call
Zimmerli finds a core in 2:1-8 with later additions in the scroll scene.

title: The scroll, the watchman and the silence
sum: Ezekiel eats the scroll, and it tastes as sweet as honey. He is told that his people are harder to move than foreigners with strange speech, and that his face will be made harder than theirs. A spirit lifts him and takes him to the exiles at Tel-abib, where he sits stunned for seven days.

Then the LORD makes him a watchman: if he warns the wicked and the righteous, he saves his own life whether or not they turn; if he stays silent, their blood is on his hands. He is shut up in his house, tied with ropes, and made mute, except when the LORD speaks through him.
readings: Read as a prophet's duty
The watchman image gives the prophet a task that does not depend on results. This is a common reading, taking the watchman as the pattern of the faithful messenger.
Read as the book's rule of responsibility

Together with chapter 18 and 33:1-20, 3:16-21 sets out the rule that each person answers for his or her own life and that the watchman answers for the warning. The three passages are best read together.

views.H: The seven days of silence at Tel-abib come before the long period of sign acts; Ezekiel is not heard until the siege is near.
views.C: Zimmerli sees 3:16-21 as a later insertion drawn from chapter 33; Greenberg and Block read it as original, with chapter 33 as its repeat.
views.J: Greenberg's 1958 study takes the muteness as a limit on reproof or intercession rather than total silence.
views.X: Paul compares himself to a watchman free of the blood of all (Acts 20:26-27); Gregory the Great applies the watchman to pastors.

echoes: Ezekiel 33:1-20; Ezekiel 18; Isaiah 21:6-12; Jeremiah 6:17; Habakkuk 2:1; Acts 20:26-27; Hebrews 13:17

settings.to: Ezekiel, for the sake of the whole house of Israel
settings.when: At the end of the seven days at Tel-abib (3:15-16), 593 BC
settings.why: To say what the prophet is accountable for. He will not be asked to make anyone listen, but he will be asked whether he warned. The charge also tells the exiles that the prophet among them has the responsibility of a lookout, and it prepares them to take his later oracles of doom seriously.
settings.readers: Repeated in 33:1-9 after the fall of Jerusalem, where it is the basis for the prophet's renewed role.
views: Original here
Block and Greenberg read it as part of the call.
Moved here from chapter 33
Zimmerli thinks a later hand put it here.

settings.what: The command to be shut in and mute
settings.when: Soon after the seven days, 593 BC
settings.why: To limit what the prophet may do until the LORD gives him words: he will not reprove or plead on his own. The muteness tells the exiles that a prophet who cannot speak for himself speaks only for God.
settings.readers: Ends with the arrival of the news of the fall of Jerusalem in 33:21-22.
views: Total silence
The prophet could not speak at all except when the LORD spoke.
A limit on his role
Greenberg: he could not act as reprover or arbiter.

title: The model of the siege
sum: In the first of the sign acts, Ezekiel is told to scratch Jerusalem on a clay brick, build a toy siege against it and set up an iron plate as a wall between himself and the city. Then he is to lie bound on his left side for 390 days, bearing the guilt of Israel, and on his right side for 40 days for Judah, with his arm bare.
He eats a small ration of mixed grain, baked on human dung. When he objects as a priest, the LORD lets him use cow dung. The act ends with the threat to break the staff of bread in Jerusalem.
readings: Read as acted prophecy
The acts happened as described, in public, and are what the book says: signs for the house of Israel. Zimmerli and Block take them this way (see the note at 4:3).
Read as a vision or literary scene

Some scholars think some of the acts were visionary or literary scenes. The day count is sometimes raised in this debate, but a leap month leaves room for 437 days between the dates of 1:2 and 8:1, and the text does not say when the acts ended (see the note at 4:5).

views.H: The siege (588-586) is still more than four years away; the acts warn the exiles of what is coming for the city they believe in.
views.C: Whether the Hebrew 390 or the Greek 190 is original is argued (see the variant at 4:5). The Hebrew 390 + 40 = 430 matches the years in Egypt (Exodus 12:40), which some commentators think is intended; the Greek totals 230. In 1946 Edwin Broome explained the acts as symptoms of illness (Ezekiel's Abnormal Personality); the text itself presents them as commanded by the LORD.
views.X: Peter's answer to the command to eat in Acts 10:14 repeats Ezekiel's protest in nearly the same words (see the note at 4:14).

echoes: Leviticus 26:26; Numbers 14:34; Exodus 12:40; Leviticus 10:17; Deuteronomy 23:12-14; Hosea 9:3-4; Acts 10:14; Isaiah 20:2-4; Jeremiah 19:1-13

settings.to: The exiles who came to watch, and through them the people of Jerusalem
settings.when: After the seven days and the command to be shut in, in or after 593 BC
settings.why: To make the exiles see the siege before it happens. They believed Jerusalem was safe; the brick with its ramps and rams, and the iron wall of the prophet's own face turned against it, say that the LORD himself is the besieger.
settings.readers: For readers after 586, the act showed that the fall was foretold and deliberate.
views: Performed in public
Most commentators.
A literary or visionary scene
Some scholars, who point to the dates.

settings.what: Lying on his side for the guilt of Israel and Judah
settings.when: For 390 and 40 days after the model, according to the Hebrew
settings.why: To show that the exile is the people's own guilt coming due, and that the prophet carries a share of its weight. The ropes show that he cannot escape the task.
settings.readers: Later readers saw the days as years of guilt or as a link to the wilderness and Egypt.
views: Years of guilt
A day for a year, as in Numbers 14:34.
The Greek count
Swete's Greek has 190 days for Israel.

settings.to: The exiles, and the priestly circle around Ezekiel
settings.why: To show life under siege: bread by weight and water by measure, and the unclean bread of the nations.
settings.readers: After 586, this recalled what the people of Jerusalem actually suffered.
views: A real ration
The weights and measures (twenty shekels of bread and a sixth of a hin of water a day) are a starvation diet, and fuel of dung is the sort of thing a siege brings (compare Lamentations 4:4-10).
A picture of defilement
The unclean bread stands for life among the nations (4:13), and the LORD's change from human to cow dung shows that the priest's rules still hold (4:14-15).

title: Razor, scales and fire
sum: Ezekiel is to shave his head and beard with a sword, divide the hair in scales, and treat the thirds differently: one third burned in the fire, one third struck with the sword, one third scattered to the wind, with a few hairs tied in his robe and even some of those burned.

Then the sign is explained. Jerusalem has been set at the center of the nations and has broken God's rulings more than they did. The LORD himself is against her. He will do what he has never done, and what he will never do again; fathers will eat sons. A third will die of plague and famine, a third by the sword, a third will be scattered. 'Then they will know that I, the LORD, have spoken.'
readings: Read as a plain threat
The chapter is an announcement that the siege will end in famine, sword and exile. The details look forward to the events of 586 BC.
Read through Leviticus 26
The chapter follows the curses of Leviticus 26 closely. The punishment is not a surprise: it was named in the covenant.

views.H: The siege, the cannibalism of a famine city and the scattering of survivors all have parallels in 2 Kings 25, Lamentations and Jeremiah 52.
views.C: The mixed prose of acts and oracle suggests layers; Zimmerli sees the explanation (5:5-17) as expanded by disciples.
views.J: Later Jewish tradition made Jerusalem the center of the world; in Ezekiel the point is the duty that goes with the place.
views.X: Revelation 6:8 lists sword, famine, death and the wild animals of the earth, the same four judgments as Ezekiel 14:21; this chapter's wild animals and plague are in 5:17.

echoes: Leviticus 26:22-33; Deuteronomy 28:53-57; Lamentations 4:10; Isaiah 7:20; Zechariah 13:8-9; Ezekiel 38:12

deep.h: A change of genre inside the chapter
deep.b: Verses 1-4 are a sign act in prose, told as commands to the prophet. At verse 5 the speech changes to a formal oracle ('The Lord GOD says this'), and in verses 11-17 it turns to oaths and curses. Readers who find 'layers' here are noticing this change; others see one speech built in three steps.

settings.what: The shaved hair divided in thirds
settings.why: To act out the end of the siege: how the people will die or be scattered.
settings.readers: A key to the three ends of 586.
views: Sign of three fates
The hair divided in thirds is explained in 5:12 as death by plague and famine, death by the sword, and scattering.
The few saved, and burned again
The hairs tied in the hem of the robe are partly burned (5:3-4), so even the survivors are not safe (see the note at 5:4).

settings.to: The exiles hearing about Jerusalem; Jerusalem itself is addressed
settings.when: With the sign, in or after 593 BC
settings.why: To say that the siege will be an act of the LORD, not a failure of his power, and that the cause is the people's conduct. It answers the exiles' belief that Jerusalem is safe.
settings.readers: After 586 it served as the book's explanation of the fall.
views: Jerusalem held to a higher standard
5:5-7 charges Jerusalem with doing worse than the nations, because she was given the LORD's rulings.
The curses of Leviticus 26 come due
5:12 and 5:16-17 follow the covenant curses (see the note at 5:17).

title: To the mountains of Israel
sum: For the first time Ezekiel speaks to the land itself. He is to face the mountains of Israel and prophesy against them: a sword is coming on the high places, the altars will be ruined, and the slain will fall in front of their filthy idols.

A few will be left alive among the nations, and they will remember the LORD, whom they have wounded, and will be disgusted by what they did. The prophet is told to strike his hands, stamp his foot and cry 'Alas!' The whole land will be a waste, and the refrain 'Then they will know that I am the LORD' comes four times.
readings: Read as a judgment on shrines
The land is addressed because its hills held the shrines. Judgment falls on the places of the worship.
Read as a first note of hope
Verses 8-10 leave room for survivors who remember. The chapter ends with desolation but sets up the later hope for the mountains of Israel in 36:1-15.

views.H: 2 Kings 23:8-20 says Josiah tore down the high places across Judah about 622 BC, yet Ezekiel's oracle, thirty years later, still speaks of them (6:3, 6, 13). The sources do not say whether the shrines were rebuilt or never fully ended (compare Jeremiah 2:20; 3:6).
views.C: The mountains of Israel (6:2-3) are a theme taken up in 36:1-15, where the same mountains are told to be fruitful; scholars see the two as paired.

echoes: Leviticus 26:30; Deuteronomy 12:2-3; 2 Kings 23:8-20; Ezekiel 36:1-15; Jeremiah 2:20; Hosea 4:13; Numbers 15:39

deep.h: 'Then they will know that I am the LORD'
deep.b: This sentence is the refrain of Ezekiel. Counted in the Hebrew, a form of 'know' is followed directly by 'that I am the LORD' in 56 verses, and by 'that I am the Lord GOD' in five more (13:9; 23:49; 24:24; 28:24; 29:16): 61 in all. In some of them the Plain reads 'that I, the LORD, have spoken' or names another act of God after the verb (5:13; 17:21; 20:12; 21:5; 22:22; 34:30; 35:12; 36:36; 37:14). Other verses have the shorter 'I, the LORD, have spoken' without 'know' (5:15, 17; 21:17, 32; 22:14; 24:14; 26:14; 30:12; 34:24). It comes at the end of oracles of judgment (6:7, 10, 13, 14; 7:4, 27) and of rescue (34:27; 36:11, 38; 37:6, 13) alike. Walther Zimmerli gave it the name 'recognition formula' (Erweiswort) and showed that it is the book's own explanation of its events: what happens, good or bad, is what makes the LORD known. In chapters 1 to 7 it is always about judgment, and the recognition it promises is not a conversion but a discovery. The Plain keeps the sentence the same each time, so that the reader can hear it return.

settings.what: Oracle to the mountains of Israel
settings.to: The mountains, hills, ravines and valleys of Israel, and through them the people of the land and the exiles who will hear it
settings.when: After the sign acts, between 593 and 592 BC (the next date is 8:1)
settings.why: To tell the exiles that the shrines they remember with affection, on the hills of their homeland, will be destroyed, and that the dead will lie among the idols. It also tells survivors what they will learn.
settings.readers: For the generation after 586, the oracle explained why the land lay waste and why a few survived.
views: Spoken to the land
The mountains are addressed as the place of the shrines.
Spoken for the people
The land stands for those who live on it.

title: The end has come
sum: In a poem of short, hammering lines, the LORD tells the land of Israel that the end has come on its four corners. The day is near, with panic on the mountains, and the LORD will pour out his anger and judge the people by their ways. The sword is outside; plague and famine are inside.

People will throw silver in the streets, put on sackcloth and shave their heads. They will look for a vision, teaching and counsel, and find none. The king will mourn, the leader will be dressed in horror, and the people of the land will tremble.
readings: Read as a funeral song for the land
The poem is built from repeated words and sounds (qets, 'end'; ba, 'comes') like a lament with the singer already standing at the grave.
Read as a collage of earlier sayings
The chapter contains lines with echoes of Amos 8:2, Zephaniah 1 and Leviticus 26; some commentators think it is made of separate oracles stitched together.

views.H: The end in view is the end of the kingdom of Judah in 586 BC; the 'king' is perhaps Zedekiah and the 'leader' a high official of his court.
views.C: The chapter is one of the hardest in the book: several words are unique, the Greek differs widely, and the Hebrew has repetition that suggests parallel versions (7:3-4 and 7:8-9).

echoes: Amos 8:1-3; Genesis 6:13; Zephaniah 1:14-18; Leviticus 25:13-28; Numbers 17:8; Jeremiah 18:18; Lamentations 2:9; Isaiah 2:20

deep.b: Chapters 1 to 6 are prose: the vision, the commission, the sign acts and the oracle to the mountains. Chapter 7 is poetry from 7:2, in short lines, with the same phrases repeated (7:3-4 and 7:8-9 are nearly the same). It is a different voice, near to the laments, and the Plain marks its lines.

settings.what: The end for the land of Israel
settings.by: The Lord GOD, in a poem
settings.to: The land of Israel, meaning its people in Judah, and the exiles listening
settings.when: After the sign acts and the mountains oracle, between 593 and 592 BC
settings.why: To tell the people, in the language of a funeral song, that the time of judgment has arrived: no wealth, vision or leader can stop it. It also removes the hope that the prophets or priests will have an answer.
settings.readers: After 586, it read as a record that the fall was foretold.
views: Spoken before the fall
The poem speaks of the end as still coming (7:6, 12), and the chapter is dated by its place in the book to the years before 586.
Shaped in more than one stage
The doubled lines (7:3-4 and 7:8-9) and the rare words have led commentators to see parallel versions or later additions.
